source.title: The Madrid Codex: New Approaches to Understanding an Ancient Maya Manuscript
source.editors: Gabrielle Vail and Anthony F. Aveni

methodological_points.claim: Aveni identifies 15 numerically cognate Dresden/Madrid almanac pairs by black-number temporal interval pattern and studies editorial revisions and relative dating.
He evaluates an approximately 131-year later Madrid M.10a-13a version of a dated Dresden D.38b-41b astronomical/seasonal almanac; dates are interpretive fits, some competing possibilities.
Vail and Victoria Bricker identify about 40 possible Haab dates beyond previously recognized Calendar Round M.73b, challenging the assumption all Madrid almanacs are exclusively 260-day divination.
Madrid 65-72 plus 73b spans 260 date signs, with 13 Ahau 13 Cumku as Calendar Round terminal glyph; the assigned Gregorian year 1451 relies on separate scholarly evidence/interpretation.
A date may be given as 13 Ik 9 Ceh in Mayapan convention and 13 Ik 10 Ceh in Classic notation; the sacred 260-day 13 Ik is unchanged.
Marriage themes in some cognate almanacs cannot be treated as natal marriage compatibility forecasts; astronomical tables and ritual timing are separate method classes.

Do not conflate 40 *possible* Haab source witnesses with 40 independently decoded glyph checks
